chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all together from Ibn Mahboub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

One of the progeny of Zurara asked him (peace be upon him) about a man who cut the tongue of a mute man. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'If his mother gave birth to him and he was mute, then upon him is a third of the wergild; and if his tongue was lost due to illness or affliction after he had been speaking, then upon the one who cut his tongue is a third of the wergild of his tongue.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And similarly is the judgement regarding the two eyes and the limbs.'
He (peace be upon him) said: 'This is how we found it in the Book of Ali (peace be upon him).'
ai.seo_question: What is the diya compensation for cutting the tongue of a mute person versus someone who lost their tongue due to illness?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between congenital and acquired disabilities, establishing that compensation for severing the tongue is one-third of the full diya regardless of whether the victim was born mute or became so later, a principle Imam al-Sadiq (AS) extends to the eyes and other limbs. It reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on precise valuation of bodily functions (ajza') within the framework of qisas and diya, ensuring equitable restitution based on the specific loss of utility rather than just the physical part. The narration underscores the continuity of legal reasoning from the Prophet’s era through the Imams, as noted by the reference to the Book of Ali (AS).

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, both together from Ibn Mahboub, from Hisham Bin Salim, from Abu Baseer, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup>, said,

‘One of the progeny of Zurara asked him<sup>asws</sup> about a man who cut the tongue of a mute man. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If it was such that his mother gave birth to him and he was mute, so upon him is a third of the wergild; and if it was such that his tongue went with away by illness or affliction after him having spoken beforehand, so upon the one who cut his tongue is a third of the wergild of his tongue; and similar to that is the judgement regarding the two eyes, and the limbs’.
He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘This is how we<sup>asws</sup> found it to be in the Book of Ali<sup>asws</sup>’.
